expected.tagline: Free, open-source sim racing in your browser: 500 Hz physics, open-wheelers and a GT3, AI races, multiplayer and wheel force feedback. Nothing to install.

installSteps.text: Alternatively, download LibreCorsa: free open-source racing simulator in your browser directly from the official site at https://librecorsa.org/. Always download from the official source — third-party mirrors of free games are a common malware vector.

Run the downloaded installer and follow the prompts. If Windows SmartScreen warns about an unrecognised publisher, that is normal for open-source projects without a paid code-signing certificate — choose More info, then Run anyway.
Open the downloaded .dmg and drag the app into Applications. On first launch macOS may refuse to open it as unidentified — right-click the app and choose Open to approve it once.
Check your distribution's package manager first, which is usually the easiest route. Otherwise download the AppImage from the official site, mark it executable and run it.

Launch the game and look at the settings menu before your first session — resolution and control defaults are worth checking. LibreCorsa: free open-source racing simulator in your browser needs roughly small of free disk space.

set.tagline: A browser racing sim with wet tyres, wheel feedback, ghost laps, and private races. Bring a pad, a wheel, or just a tab.
set.description: LibreCorsa puts open-wheel cars, GT3 machines, changing weather, AI races, and online rooms into a browser tab. Chase a ghost lap, race a friend, or learn a circuit in the rain. Keyboard, gamepad, touch, and compatible wheels are supported; the game costs nothing and needs no install.

systemRequirements.min: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, or iOS · modern WebGL2-capable browser · keyboard, gamepad, touch, or compatible wheel · internet connection for online play. The developer has not published minimum CPU, RAM, GPU, or storage figures.
systemRequirements.recommended: No recommended CPU, RAM, GPU, or storage tier has been published. Chrome or Edge on desktop supports the experimental WebHID wheel force-feedback path; a compatible gamepad works through the browser Gamepad API.

qualityBar.verdict: A racing sim with enough tyre and track detail to make the first wet kerb matter, running in the tab you were about to close.

set.longDescription:
LibreCorsa starts with an unusually small request for a racing sim: open a browser tab. From there, it offers the things that usually demand a large install and a long settings session: open-wheel cars, GT3 machinery, changing weather, AI grids, lap timing, replays, and private races. You can take a road car out to learn a circuit, move to a prototype when you want a quicker lesson, or put a race car onto a wet track and discover that your dry braking marker has become a bad suggestion.

The driving model is the project's obsession. Vehicle dynamics run at a fixed 500 Hz, with tyre temperature, pressure, wear, suspension geometry, aero load, and different surfaces all affecting the result. Those details are useful because they give a driver something to respond to. A kerb has a shape and a grip level; rain builds on the road and the racing line dries as cars circulate. Assists can make keyboard or pad steering less punishing, while drivers who want more work can tune the car and turn the help down. A compatible force-feedback wheel can carry some of that surface information back to your hands, although the developer is candid that wheel support varies by device and browser.

There is more to do than hot-lap alone. AI races have adjustable difficulty and traffic to navigate. A saved personal-best ghost lets you see exactly where a cleaner exit gained time, and a short instant replay gives you another view of a mistake. Online boards record laps by circuit and car. For company, you can host a private peer-to-peer room and share its link or six-character code, or join an open race on the game's schedule. Everyone in a room needs the same game version. No PlayBound-hosted dedicated server is required for these browser races.

The easy entry is a real advantage, but it does not erase the edges of a fast-moving solo project. There are no published hardware tiers, and experimental wheel feedback is not a promise for every base. If the exact behaviour of a wheel matters to you, check the project's tested-device list before planning a session around it. If you simply want to drive, a keyboard, pad, or touch screen gets you onto the track without an installer. LibreCorsa is at its best when that convenience leads into a serious attempt to shave a corner, not when it is treated as a technical novelty.
set.whyWePickedIt: A free browser game rarely gives us a reason to discuss tyre behaviour, force feedback, and private racing rooms in the same breath. LibreCorsa does. It makes a demanding kind of PC play approachable without flattening the driving into a disposable minigame, and it lets friends race without buying matching copies or arranging a server. The open source code and the developer's clear notes about unfinished wheel compatibility make it easier to recommend honestly. We want players to find projects like this while they are still growing.
set.thatOneThing: Your old best lap becomes a ghost, so the corner you keep blaming on the car can testify against you.

installSteps.text: Open librecorsa.org in a modern browser and choose Drive. The game runs in the tab; no desktop installer is needed.

firstPlaySteps.text: Choose a car and circuit, then use the in-game controls menu to configure a keyboard, gamepad, touch screen, or compatible wheel.
Start with the default assists and an AI practice race or a hot lap. Adjust realism and input settings as you learn the car.

multiplayerGamingSteps.text: Open Multiplayer in LibreCorsa, host a private room, and send its invite link or six-character code to a friend. They join in their own browser.
For an open race, use the scheduled race card. Private rooms are peer-to-peer; every player needs the same game version.

bestFor: Racing fans who want to practice laps without installing a large sim
Friends who want an easy private race across their browsers
Drivers who enjoy tuning assists, weather, and input devices
notFor: Players who need published hardware benchmarks before trying a game
Wheel owners who require guaranteed force feedback on every device

faq.q: Do I need to install LibreCorsa?
faq.a: No. It runs at librecorsa.org in a modern browser. The PlayBound launcher opens the game's site.
Yes. Host a private room and share its link or six-character code. LibreCorsa also runs scheduled open races.

faq.q: Does it support controllers and wheels?
faq.a: Gamepads work through the browser Gamepad API. Wheel input is supported, while force-feedback compatibility varies by device and browser and remains experimental.

faq.q: Does PlayBound host a dedicated server for it?
faq.a: No. LibreCorsa's private browser races use peer-to-peer rooms. Host a room in the game and share its invite link or code.
